message.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Small undulatory swimmers such as larval zebrafish experience both inertial and viscous forces, the relative importance of which is indicated by the Reynolds number (
                    <jats:italic>Re</jats:italic>
                    ).
                    <jats:italic>Re</jats:italic>
                    is proportional to swimming speed (
                    <jats:italic>v</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>swim</jats:sub>
                    ) and body length; faster swimming reduces the relative effect of viscous forces. Compared with adults, larval fish experience relatively high (mainly viscous) drag during cyclic swimming. To enhance thrust to an equally high level, they must employ a high product of tail-beat frequency and (peak-to-peak) amplitude
                    <jats:italic>fA</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>tail</jats:sub>
                    , resulting in a relatively high
                    <jats:italic>
                      fA
                      <jats:sub>
                        <jats:italic>tail</jats:italic>
                      </jats:sub>
                      /
                      <jats:overline>v</jats:overline>
                      <jats:sub>
                        <jats:italic>swim</jats:italic>
                      </jats:sub>
                    </jats:italic>
                    ratio (Strouhal number, St), and implying relatively high lateral momentum shedding and low propulsive efficiency. Using kinematic and inverse-dynamics analyses, we studied cyclic swimming of larval zebrafish aged 2–5 days post-fertilization (dpf). Larvae at 4–5 dpf reach higher
                    <jats:italic>f</jats:italic>
                    (95 Hz) and
                    <jats:italic>A</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>tail</jats:sub>
                    (2.4 mm) than at 2 dpf (80 Hz, 1.8 mm), increasing swimming speed and
                    <jats:italic>Re</jats:italic>
                    , indicating increasing muscle powers. As
                    <jats:italic>Re</jats:italic>
                    increases (60 → 1400), St (2.5 → 0.72) decreases nonlinearly towards values of large swimmers (0.2–0.6), indicating increased propulsive efficiency with
                    <jats:italic>v</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>swim</jats:sub>
                    and age. Swimming at high St is associated with high-amplitude body torques and rotations. Low propulsive efficiencies and large yawing amplitudes are unavoidable physical constraints for small undulatory swimmers.
                  </jats:p>
title: How body torque and Strouhal number change with swimming speed and developmental stage in larval zebrafish
